questions.q: A project manager is managing a product launch in a foreign market with strict regulatory requirements. What should the project manager do to ensure compliance? *

o.t: Conduct a regulatory impact assessment early in the project.
Wait for regulatory agencies to provide feedback before making changes.
Assign a team member to research regulations at the end of development.
Delay the launch until the legal team completes a final review.

questions.e: Proactively conducting a regulatory impact assessment early helps the team anticipate compliance issues and integrate necessary requirements from the start.

questions.q: A project manager conducted an analysis with relevant stakeholders to determine the benefits of a proposed project. During the analysis, different stakeholders provided conflicting opinions on the expected benefits. What should the project manager pay attention to? *

o.t: Formal approval of project change requests is required before making decisions.
Stakeholder dissatisfaction with key project deliverables may occur.
Conflict in subsequent phases of the project may delay execution.
Inconsistent input on benefits from key stakeholders may lead to misalignment with business objectives.

questions.e: One of the key importance of project management is ensuring that stakeholder expectations align with business objectives. If different stakeholders provide inconsistent benefits, it could cause misalignment and lead to confusion in decision-making.

questions.q: A project sponsor requests an increase in project scope without adjusting the budget or timeline. According to the concept of competing constraints, which of the following is the most likely impact on the project? *

o.t: Project quality may decrease due to resource limitations.
The project will be completed successfully without any impact if regular meetings are held.
The project team will have to request additional funding.
The project schedule will be shortened to accommodate the change.

questions.e: In competing constraints, if one constraint (e.g., scope) increases without adjusting other factors (time and cost), it can negatively impact other areas, such as quality. Since the project budget and timeline remain the same, the team may have to cut corners or reduce quality to meet the expanded scope. Scope, time, cost, quality, risk, and resources must be balanced to ensure project success.

questions.q: A large multinational organization has a centralized PMO that fully manages projects by assigning project managers and directly overseeing execution. What type of PMO is this? *

o.t: Supportive PMO
Controlling PMO
Directive PMO
Strategic PMO

questions.e: A Directive PMO has high authority over projects and directly manages their execution. It assigns project managers, controls resources, and ensures full compliance with project management standards. This model is typically used in highly structured organizations where project success is critical to business operations.

questions.q: How does portfolio management differ from project and program management within an organization? *

o.t: Portfolio management focuses on coordinating related projects to achieve benefits that wouldn’t be possible if managed separately.
Portfolio management ensures that projects and programs align with organizational strategy and business objectives.
Portfolio management involves managing only one project at a time to maximize efficiency.
Portfolio management focuses on delivering technical solutions to strategic stakeholders in a timely manner.

questions.e: Portfolio management focuses on selecting, prioritizing, and managing projects and programs to ensure they align with organizational goals and strategic objectives. Program management coordinates related projects to achieve synergies and benefits. Project management focuses on delivering a specific product, service, or result within defined constraints (scope, time, cost, etc.). Portfolio management operates at a higher level, ensuring that investments in projects and programs support business success rather than just individual project outcomes.

questions.q: A project manager notices a key stakeholder is actively resisting the project. What is the most effective first step to improve engagement? *

o.t: Increase stakeholder communication frequency
Escalate the issue to senior management
Meet with the stakeholder to understand concerns
Remove the stakeholder from the engagement plan

questions.e: Understanding the stakeholder's concerns is crucial to developing an effective engagement strategy. Direct communication helps uncover the root cause of resistance and fosters collaboration.

questions.q: A key stakeholder in your project has been unresponsive to emails and meeting requests. However, they have significant influence over the project and could impact final approvals. What is the best course of action? *

o.t: Escalate the issue to senior management and request their intervention.
Continue sending emails and wait for the stakeholder to respond.
Arrange an informal meeting or approach them through a preferred communication channel.
Remove the stakeholder from the engagement plan since they are unresponsive.

questions.e: Some stakeholders may prefer face-to-face interactions or a different communication style. Understanding their preferences and engaging them personally can help ensure their involvement in the project.

questions.q: A key external stakeholder in your project has a history of strongly opposing similar initiatives. How should you proactively engage them? *

o.t: Avoid involving them in discussions to prevent potential conflicts.
Keep them informed with project updates but minimize their decision-making role.
Involve them early and address concerns before opposition arises.
Request higher management to override their objections.

questions.e: Proactively engaging resistant stakeholders helps mitigate risks and prevents escalated conflicts later in the project.

questions.q: A project is at risk due to conflicting stakeholder expectations. The sponsor wants cost savings, the team wants innovation, and end-users prioritize usability. How should you manage this situation? *

o.t: Organize stakeholder workshops to align expectations and reach a balanced solution.
Prioritize the sponsor’s expectations since they provide funding.
Reduce engagement with conflicting stakeholders to minimize disruption.
Adjust the project plan to accommodate all expectations, even if it increases risk.

questions.e: Facilitating collaboration through workshops helps stakeholders understand trade-offs and align their priorities.

questions.q: A high-power, low-interest stakeholder has requested major project changes that would impact cost and schedule. What is the best way to handle this? *

o.t: Implement the changes immediately since they have high power.
Politely decline their request to maintain the original project plan.
Evaluate the feasibility and propose alternatives that minimize impact.
Escalate the request to the project sponsor without further discussion.

questions.e: Stakeholders with high power require careful management. Evaluating their requests and offering alternative solutions ensures engagement while protecting project constraints.

questions.q: A project team is struggling with motivation, and deadlines are being missed. The project manager decides to use a leadership approach that focuses on coaching, mentoring, and developing individual team members. What type of leadership style is being applied? *

o.t: Autocratic
Servant Leadership
Transactional
Laissez-Faire

questions.e: Servant leadership focuses on developing, coaching, and mentoring team members to help them reach their full potential. This approach builds motivation by empowering and supporting the team.

questions.q: A project team is struggling with meeting deadlines due to unclear task responsibilities and lack of coordination. Team members frequently escalate minor issues instead of resolving them independently. What leadership approach should the project manager take to improve team performance? *

o.t: Use a directive (authoritative) leadership style to assign tasks and enforce strict controls.
Encourage servant leadership by mentoring the team and fostering collaboration.
Adopt a laissez-faire approach and let the team self-organize.
Increase the use of coercive power to ensure compliance with deadlines.

questions.e: The servant leadership approach would help develop team capabilities by guiding them toward self-sufficiency. By coaching and mentoring, the project manager can clarify roles, encourage collaboration, and improve problem-solving within the team. A directive style (A) may create dependency rather than empowerment. Laissez-faire leadership (C) might lead to further disorganization. Coercive power (D) would likely damage morale and reduce engagement.

questions.q: A project manager is facilitating a brainstorming session where team members need to generate new ideas and collaborate dynamically. What is the most effective communication approach? *

o.t: Interactive in-person or virtual meeting with real-time idea-sharing tools
Sending a questionnaire via email and collecting responses later
Writing a report with a list of proposed ideas
Sending individual messages to each team member asking for suggestions

questions.e: Brainstorming sessions require real-time collaboration and dynamic discussion. Interactive meetings with idea-sharing tools (e.g., virtual whiteboards, chat apps) foster engagement and creativity.

questions.q: Your project team is struggling with collaboration due to unclear responsibilities, and team members frequently duplicate work or miss critical tasks. What is the best approach to improve collaboration? *

o.t: Implement a RACI matrix to define roles and responsibilities clearly.
Schedule more meetings to increase team discussions.
Assign a single team lead to oversee all task coordination.
Allow the team to self-organize and resolve role conflicts independently.

questions.e: A RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) matrix helps eliminate confusion by clearly defining who is responsible for what tasks. Increasing meetings (B) may not address the root issue of unclear roles. Assigning a single team lead (C) might reduce collaboration rather than improve it. Self-organizing teams (D) work well in Agile but need clear role definitions to avoid duplication and gaps.

questions.q: A conflict arises between two team members over decision-making authority. The tension is affecting collaboration and slowing down progress. As the project manager, how should you handle this situation? *

o.t: Clearly define roles and decision-making responsibilities to prevent future conflicts.
Ask the team members to resolve the issue on their own.
Remove one of the team members from the project to reduce conflict.
Escalate the issue to HR for resolution.

questions.e: Role clarity is essential to prevent authority conflicts. Clearly outlining who has decision-making power eliminates confusion and promotes collaboration. Letting them resolve it alone (B) may lead to ongoing disputes. Removing a team member (C) is unnecessary unless performance is severely impacted. HR escalation (D) should be a last resort.

questions.q: A company is transitioning from Waterfall to Agile but faces resistance from senior leadership, who are accustomed to fixed schedules and upfront planning. How can the Agile team address this resistance? *

o.t: Provide Agile training and demonstrate how iterative planning delivers value incrementally.
Implement Agile practices without informing leadership to avoid conflict.
Maintain the existing Waterfall approach to align with leadership preferences.
Stop engaging with leadership and focus only on team-level Agile adoption.

questions.e: Resistance to Agile is common when leaders are used to predictive approaches. Training and demonstrating Agile’s benefits through incremental value delivery help build buy-in. Avoiding leadership (B, D) creates misalignment. Keeping Waterfall (C) contradicts the Agile transition goal.

questions.q: A development team is working on a product that requires frequent updates based on real-time user feedback. The team wants to release new features continuously rather than waiting for fixed intervals. Which delivery cadence best supports this approach? *

o.t: Continuous Delivery (CD)
Iteration-Based Delivery
Time-Boxed Sprints
Program Increment (PI) Planning

questions.e: Continuous Delivery (CD) ensures that new features, bug fixes, and updates are released to production frequently—sometimes multiple times a day. Iteration-Based Delivery (B) and Time-Boxed Sprints (C) follow fixed intervals, which do not align with the need for real-time updates. Program Increment (PI) Planning (D) is used in scaled Agile frameworks like SAFe but is not meant for continuous releases.

questions.q: A Scrum Team consistently fails to meet the Definition of Done (DoD) at the end of each Sprint. What should be the first step to address this issue? *

o.t: Review and refine the Definition of Done to ensure it is realistic.
Extend the Sprint length to allow more time for completion.
Exclude non-completed work from the DoD and release the remaining deliverables.
Assign additional team members to ensure all work meets the DoD.

questions.e: The DoD must be clear, achievable, and agreed upon by the team. Reviewing and refining it ensures alignment with capabilities and expectations.

questions.q: A Scrum Team is struggling with a growing Product Backlog that contains hundreds of items. Many of these items have not been reviewed in months, and the team is unsure which items to focus on. What should the Scrum Master encourage the team to do? *

o.t: Conduct regular backlog refinement sessions to prioritize and remove outdated items.
Archive older backlog items to reduce the backlog size.
Prioritize backlog items based only on the Scrum Team’s preferences.
Start with the oldest backlog items first, ensuring all work is completed in sequence.

questions.e: Backlog refinement is crucial to keeping the Product Backlog relevant and ensuring that work aligns with business priorities. Simply archiving (B) items without review may remove valuable features. Prioritization should be business-driven rather than based on team preference (C). Working strictly in chronological order (D) ignores changing business needs.

questions.q: What is the key difference between an MVP and an MMP in Agile product development? *

o.t: An MVP is used for market entry, while an MMP is for internal testing.
An MVP is a test version to gather feedback, while an MMP is a release-ready product for customers.
An MVP has all planned features, while an MMP has only basic features.
An MVP is released after the MMP to refine the product.

questions.e: An MVP is a learning tool with minimal features to validate assumptions and gather user feedback. An MMP is ready for the market and includes enough features to attract customers. An MVP is launched before an MMP to ensure the product concept is viable before scaling.

questions.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager to begin work on a new initiative without a formally approved project charter. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Proceed with the project since the sponsor has requested it.
Document project objectives and scope and begin execution immediately.
Inform the sponsor that the project cannot officially start without an approved charter.
Start with a stakeholder analysis while waiting for the charter approval.

questions.e: The Project Charter formally authorizes the project and provides the project manager with authority to use organizational resources. Without an approved charter, the project has no formal backing. Starting execution (A, B, D) without a charter risks misalignment and lack of authority.

questions.q: A project has limited resources, and some tasks are delayed because resource availability is constrained. The project manager needs to balance workload without exceeding available resources. Which technique should be applied? *

o.t: Resource Leveling
Critical Path Method (CPM)
Schedule Compression
Leads and Lags

questions.e: Resource Leveling adjusts activity start and finish dates to ensure resource demand does not exceed availability. CPM (B) focuses on duration, not resource constraints. Schedule Compression (C) shortens timelines but does not optimize resources. Leads and Lags (D) adjust task relationships but do not address resource limits.

questions.q: A project manager is leading a complex IT project with multiple stakeholders. During execution, a senior executive requests a significant change that affects project scope, schedule, and budget. The project manager refers to the Project Management Plan before taking action. What is the primary reason for doing this? *

o.t: To determine if the change aligns with the project’s strategic objectives.
To review the change control process and assess how the change impacts project constraints.
To obtain formal approval from the project sponsor before discussing the change with the team.
To ensure that the executive’s request is automatically incorporated into the project plan.

questions.e: The Project Management Plan includes the Change Management Plan, which defines how changes are evaluated and approved. Any change affecting scope, schedule, and budget must be formally assessed for impact before implementation. Strategic alignment (A) is important but does not replace the need for impact analysis. Obtaining sponsor approval first (C) bypasses impact assessment. Automatically incorporating changes (D) leads to uncontrolled scope creep.

questions.q: A project manager is planning a software development project where the testing phase can begin only after 50% of the coding is completed. Which type of dependency and lag should be used to model this relationship? *

o.t: Start-to-Start (SS) with a 50% progress milestone
Finish-to-Finish (FF) with a lead time
Finish-to-Start (FS) with a lag time
Start-to-Finish (SF) with a dependency buffer

questions.e: Start-to-Start (SS) means two activities can start at different times but overlap. Since testing can begin after 50% of coding is complete, it indicates a partial dependency rather than waiting for full completion. Finish-to-Finish (FF) (B) would require both to finish together, which is incorrect. Finish-to-Start (FS) (C) means testing would have to wait for full completion, which is not the case. Start-to-Finish (SF) (D) is an unusual dependency and does not apply here.

questions.q: A project team is working on a government project with strict regulatory requirements. A regulatory agency mandates a change that affects a key deliverable. How should the project manager handle this change? *

o.t: Implement the change immediately since it is a regulatory requirement.
Perform an impact analysis and follow the formal change control process.
Reject the change if it was not part of the original contract.
Escalate the issue to senior management and let them handle the decision.

questions.e: Even regulatory changes must go through formal change control. Impact analysis identifies schedule, cost, and risk implications before implementation. Automatically implementing changes (A) without analysis can lead to resource constraints. Rejecting the change (C) is unrealistic for regulatory compliance projects. Escalation to senior management (D) should happen only after the project team has assessed the impact.

questions.q: A project team is struggling to understand the detailed needs of an end-user group. Which technique involves direct interaction with users to observe their tasks and gain real-world insights? *

o.t: Document Analysis
Job Shadowing
Surveys and Questionnaires
Affinity Diagrams

questions.e: Job shadowing involves observing end-users in their work environment, helping the project team capture actual workflows and unspoken needs. Document Analysis (A) reviews existing documents but does not provide real-time insights. Surveys (C) collect feedback but may not capture actual behaviors. Affinity Diagrams (D) categorize information but do not involve direct observation.

questions.q: A project manager breaks down the project work into detailed tasks and estimates each individually before rolling them up to determine the total project cost. What estimating technique is being used? *

o.t: Parametric Estimating
Bottom-Up Estimating
Analogous Estimating
Heuristic Estimating

questions.e: Bottom-up estimating calculates costs and effort at the lowest level (task level) and aggregates them for the total project estimate. Parametric estimating (A) relies on unit-based models rather than task aggregation. Analogous estimating (C) uses past project comparisons instead of detailed calculations. Heuristic estimating (D) uses predefined rules of thumb rather than summing detailed estimates.

questions.q: A project manager consults a panel of industry experts to estimate costs based on their experience and insights. What estimating technique is being used? *

o.t: Delphi Technique
Expert Judgment
Analogous Estimating
Monte Carlo Simulation

questions.e: Expert judgment relies on industry specialists to provide informed estimates based on their experience. Delphi Technique (A) gathers expert opinions anonymously rather than direct consultation. Analogous Estimating (C) compares historical projects rather than relying on expert opinions. Monte Carlo Simulation (D) uses statistical modeling rather than expert experience.

questions.q: A project team needs to make a decision on the best approach for executing a critical task. The project manager asks all members to vote, and the option with the highest number of votes is selected. What type of voting technique is being used? *

o.t: Majority Voting
Unanimity
Plurality Voting
Delphi Technique

questions.e: Majority voting requires more than 50% of the votes for an option to be selected. Unanimity (B) requires all members to agree. Plurality (C) selects the option with the most votes, even if it does not exceed 50%. Delphi Technique (D) involves expert consensus over multiple rounds rather than open voting.

questions.q: During schedule planning, a critical supplier informs the project manager of a potential delay in material delivery. What is the best approach? *

o.t: Accept the delay and adjust the project schedule accordingly.
Identify alternative suppliers and include a contingency plan.
Expedite the other project activities to compensate for the delay.
Escalate the issue to senior management for resolution.

questions.e: Risk management is essential in planning—identifying alternatives prevents delays. Simply accepting delays (A) without action affects project completion. Expediting other activities (C) may not mitigate the specific risk. Escalation (D) is premature without first seeking a solution.

questions.q: A project manager is executing work but finds that team members are waiting for approvals, causing bottlenecks. What technique can help accelerate decision-making? *

o.t: Delegation of Authority
Team-Building
Resource Allocation
Promote most performing resources

questions.e: Delegation of authority speeds up execution by empowering team members to make decisions within their responsibilities.

questions.q: In an Agile team, two developers work on the same piece of code together—one writing code and the other reviewing it in real-time. What technique is being used? *

o.t: Pair Programming
Swarming
Mobbing
Fast Tracking

questions.e: Pair programming involves two developers working on the same task, improving quality and reducing defects. Swarming (B) is a broader approach where multiple members work on one issue. Mobbing (C) involves the whole team collaborating. Fast tracking (D) is used for schedule compression.

questions.q: A team member intentionally withholds information to avoid blame in case of failure. What is this behavior called? *

o.t: Self-Protection
Sandbagging
Information-Keeping
Sabotaging

questions.e: Self-protection involves hiding issues or avoiding responsibility to protect oneself from blame.

questions.q: A project manager conducts a meeting at the start of a project to introduce team members, define roles, and align stakeholders on objectives. What type of meeting is this? *

o.t: Sprint Kickoff Meeting
Team-Building Meeting
Project Kickoff Meeting
Planning Meeting

questions.e: Kickoff meetings are held at the beginning of a project to introduce stakeholders, set expectations, and clarify objectives.

questions.q: A project team applies an iterative approach where they review completed work, gather feedback, and use insights to improve future work cycles. What concept does this represent? *

o.t: Learning Loops
Kaizen
Sprint Retrospectives
Continuous Integration

questions.e: Learning Loops involve cycles of execution, feedback, and improvement, allowing teams to adapt and refine their approach over time. Kaizen (B) is the philosophy of continuous improvement but does not necessarily follow a loop structure. Sprint Retrospectives (C) are Agile-specific but a type of learning loop. Continuous Integration (D) is a development practice, not an improvement framework.

questions.q: A project manager is conducting a bidder conference to ensure that all potential vendors have a clear understanding of the project requirements. What is the primary purpose of a bidder conference? *

o.t: To negotiate contract terms with the preferred vendor.
To provide all bidders with equal information and clarify project requirements.
To finalize the selection of a vendor before contract award.
To allow vendors to present their proposals before selection.

questions.e: A bidder conference (also called a pre-bid meeting) ensures all potential vendors receive the same information and clarifications, promoting fairness and competition. Negotiations (A) occur after vendor selection. Finalizing vendor selection (C) happens after proposal evaluations. Vendor presentations (D) occur in proposal reviews, not the bidder conference.

questions.q: A project manager is evaluating vendor proposals for a critical software project. The organization requires the selected vendor to have strong cybersecurity measures and regulatory compliance. What vendor selection technique should be used? *

o.t: Least Cost Selection
Weighted Scoring Model
Sole Sourcing
Procurement Negotiation

questions.e: A weighted scoring model assigns numerical values to selection criteria (e.g., security, compliance, cost, experience) to ensure the best fit. Least Cost Selection (A) is used when cost is the only factor. Sole Sourcing (C) is for non-competitive, single-vendor procurement. Procurement Negotiation (D) occurs after vendor selection.

questions.q: A project requires specialized equipment that only one vendor can provide. The project manager must select a vendor quickly to avoid delays. What is the most appropriate selection method? *

o.t: Sole Sourcing
Competitive Bidding
Best Value Selection
Reverse Auction

questions.e: Sole sourcing is used when only one vendor can provide the required product or service. Competitive Bidding (B) is for multiple vendors. Best Value (C) compares multiple factors but is unnecessary when there’s only one option. Reverse Auction (D) is for cost-based selection, which does not apply to a single vendor.

questions.q: A project manager is concerned about the quality of materials supplied by a vendor during production. The project team visits the vendor’s facility to check work-in-progress items and ensure compliance with project specifications. What type of vendor inspection is being conducted? *

o.t: In-Process Inspection
Pre-shipment Inspection
Factory Acceptance Testing
Supplier Auditing

questions.e: In-process inspections occur while the vendor is manufacturing or assembling products to ensure adherence to specifications. Pre-shipment inspections (B) happen before shipping, not during production. Factory Acceptance Testing (C) occurs when testing a completed system before delivery. Supplier Auditing (D) evaluates the vendor’s processes but does not inspect specific work items.

questions.q: A company hires a contractor to build a facility for a set price, with no additional payments allowed. The contractor assumes all cost risks. What type of contract is this? *

o.t: Cost Plus Incentive Fee (CPIF)
Fixed Price with Economic Price Adjustment (FP-EPA)
Firm Fixed Price (FFP)
Time and Materials (T&M)

questions.e: FFP contracts have a set price with no adjustments, making the contractor fully responsible for cost overruns. CPIF (A) includes incentives but is cost-reimbursable. FP-EPA (B) allows for price adjustments, which is not the case here. T&M (D) pays based on hours and materials, not a fixed price.

questions.q: A project manager notices that 80% of defects originate from 20% of process issues. What quality management technique is being applied? *

o.t: Pareto Analysis
Statistical Sampling
Control Charting
Cause-and-Effect Diagram

questions.q: A project manager wants to ensure that project processes are being followed correctly and consistently. What is the best quality assurance technique to use? *

o.t: Quality Control Inspections
Process Audits
Pareto Analysis
Statistical Sampling

questions.e: Quality assurance (QA) focuses on preventing defects by ensuring that processes are followed correctly. Process audits review adherence to quality standards, policies, and procedures. Quality control inspections (A) check the end product, not the process. Pareto Analysis (C) prioritizes defects but does not ensure process compliance. Statistical Sampling (D) inspects a subset of items but does not assess process effectiveness.

questions.q: A company is spending a significant amount on warranty claims and rework due to defective products. What should they focus on improving? *

o.t: Prevention Costs
Appraisal Costs
Internal Failure Costs
External Failure Costs

questions.e: External failure costs include warranty claims, customer complaints, and product recalls. Prevention costs (A) focus on proactive measures like training and process improvements. Appraisal costs (B) involve testing and inspections to detect defects before reaching customers. Internal failure costs (C) occur when defects are found before delivery.

questions.q: A project team is using a new manufacturing process, but defects have increased significantly. The project manager wants to determine if the variations in the process are within acceptable limits. What tool should be used? *

o.t: Fishbone Diagram
Control Charts
Pareto Analysis
Benchmarking

questions.e: Control charts help track process variations and determine if they fall within acceptable control limits. Fishbone diagrams (A) identify root causes of defects but do not monitor process variations. Pareto analysis (C) prioritizes major defect categories but does not measure stability. Benchmarking (D) compares performance with industry standards but does not track real-time variations.

questions.q: A project team is developing a high-tech product for a client with strict quality requirements. During testing, multiple defects are found in different functional areas, delaying the timeline. The client is concerned about the project’s ability to meet deadlines, while the development team argues that more testing time is needed to ensure defect-free delivery. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Increase testing frequency and focus on all defects equally.
Conduct a Pareto Analysis to prioritize defects that have the highest impact on functionality.
Request additional time from the client to complete testing without compromises.
Deliver the product with minor defects and promise to fix them in the next version.

questions.e: Pareto Analysis (80/20 rule) helps focus on critical defects first, ensuring the most significant issues are addressed without excessive delays. Increasing testing (A) without prioritization may waste time on less critical defects. Requesting more time (C) may not be feasible and could affect client satisfaction. Delivering a defective product (D) can lead to reputational damage and rework costs.

questions.q: A stakeholder is reviewing the risk management plan and asks how the team will determine which risks need urgent attention. What should the project manager refer to? *

o.t: The Probability and Impact Matrix.
The Risk Breakdown Structure (RBS).
The Project Schedule.
The Change Management Plan.

questions.e: The Probability and Impact Matrix helps prioritize risks by assigning a score based on likelihood and severity. The RBS (B) categorizes risks but does not prioritize them. The Project Schedule (C) tracks timelines, not risks. The Change Management Plan (D) manages scope changes, not risk prioritization.

questions.q: During the execution phase of a high-risk project, the project manager sets aside contingency reserves for risks that have been identified and analyzed. However, the sponsor suggests setting aside additional funds for completely unexpected risks that may arise later. What is the sponsor recommending? *

o.t: Management Reserve for Unknown Unknowns
Contingency Reserve for Known Unknowns
Risk Reassessment for Emerging Risks
Change Control Process for Scope Adjustments

questions.e: Management reserves are funds set aside for unknown unknowns—completely unforeseen risks. Contingency reserves (B) are allocated for known unknowns (identified but uncertain risks). Risk reassessment (C) is the process of reviewing and updating risk analysis, but it does not allocate funds. Change control (D) handles project scope modifications, not risk-related reserves.

questions.q: A company is launching a new product in an emerging market with no historical data or established customer behavior trends. The project team is struggling to define a clear strategy because there is no precedent or available information on how customers will react. What element is most evident in this scenario? *

o.t: Volatility
Uncertainty
Complexity
Ambiguity

questions.e: Ambiguity occurs when there is a lack of clarity about cause-and-effect relationships, making it difficult to define a clear strategy. Volatility (A) refers to fast-changing conditions, whereas this issue is more about a lack of clarity. Uncertainty (B) deals with situations where some information is missing but can be researched, whereas ambiguity refers to a complete lack of understanding. Complexity (C) relates to multiple interconnected elements, which is not the primary issue here.

questions.q: A key supplier has informed the project team that they will not be able to deliver a critical component on time, impacting the project's critical path. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Implement a previously planned risk response strategy.
Escalate the issue to procurement and wait for a resolution.
Extend the project schedule to accommodate the delay.
Terminate the contract with the supplier immediately.

questions.e: Risk response strategies (e.g., using an alternate supplier, fast-tracking) should be executed when an identified risk occurs. Escalating the issue (B) is necessary if the response plan is ineffective. Extending the schedule (C) should be a last resort. Terminating the contract (D) without an alternative could worsen the situation.

questions.q: A project manager wants to proactively reduce the probability of a major project failure. Which strategy should be applied? *

o.t: Mitigation
Avoidance
Transfer
Acceptance

questions.e: Risk avoidance eliminates the root cause of a risk to prevent its occurrence. Mitigation (A) reduces risk impact but does not eliminate it. Transfer (C) shifts responsibility but does not prevent occurrence. Acceptance (D) is a passive approach, not a proactive one.

questions.q: A project sponsor wants to assess how well a recently completed project contributed to the organization’s strategic goals. Which business performance metric should be used? *

o.t: Return on Investment (ROI)
Cost Performance Index (CPI)
Sprint Velocity
Number of Change Requests Processed

questions.e: ROI measures the financial return generated by a project relative to its cost, indicating its value to the business. CPI (B) is a project cost control measure but does not evaluate overall business impact. Sprint Velocity (C) is an Agile metric focused on development speed, not strategic alignment. Number of Change Requests (D) tracks scope changes but does not assess business performance.

questions.q: A project has a total budget of $500,000 and is planned to be 60% complete. The project manager finds that the project is actually 50% complete and has spent $290,000. What is the Schedule Performance Index (SPI)? *
questions.e: SPI = Earned Value (EV) / Planned Value (PV) EV = Budget × % Work Completed = $500,000 × 50% = $250,000 PV = Budget × % Planned Completion = $500,000 × 60% = $300,000 SPI = $250,000 / $300,000 = 0.83 Since SPI < 1, the project is behind schedule.

questions.q: A project has an Earned Value (EV) of $90,000 and a Planned Value (PV) of $100,000. What is the Schedule Variance (SV)? *
questions.e: SV = EV - PV SV = $90,000 - $100,000 = -$10,000 Since SV is negative, the project is behind schedule. Concept-Based EVM Questions

questions.q: A project has a SPI of 0.75 and a CPI of 1.05. What does this mean? *

o.t: The project is behind schedule but under budget.
The project is ahead of schedule but over budget.
The project is behind schedule and over budget.
The project is ahead of schedule and under budget.

questions.e: SPI < 1 (0.75) → The project is behind schedule. CPI > 1 (1.05) → The project is under budget.

questions.q: A project team is using Earned Value Management (EVM) to track project performance. The project manager needs to report on how efficiently resources are being used. Which metric should be highlighted in the performance report? *

o.t: Schedule Variance (SV)
Cost Performance Index (CPI)
Change Request Log
Net Promoter Score (NPS)

questions.e: CPI = Earned Value (EV) / Actual Cost (AC). If CPI > 1, the project is cost-efficient; if CPI < 1, the project is over budget. SV (A) tracks schedule efficiency, not cost efficiency. Change Request Log (C) records scope changes, not financial performance. NPS (D) measures customer satisfaction but does not relate to cost performance.

questions.q: You are managing a project that is slightly behind schedule. A senior stakeholder suggests adding extra team members to accelerate the work. What should you do first? *

o.t: Accept the suggestion and immediately assign additional team members.
Conduct a schedule impact analysis before making a decision.
Inform the stakeholder that adding more people may increase risks.
Reject the idea because adding resources late in the project is ineffective.

questions.e: Before making changes, you must analyze their impact on the schedule, budget, and resources. Option A (immediately adding people) may cause inefficiencies due to the "Brooks' Law" effect. Option C (notifying risks) is important but should come after analysis. Option D (rejecting the idea) is premature without assessing feasibility.

questions.q: A project manager is working on a government contract with strict compliance requirements. Which document should be referenced to ensure legal adherence? *

o.t: Project Charter
Risk Register
Procurement Management Plan
Compliance Management Plan

questions.e: The Compliance Management Plan ensures legal and regulatory adherence. Charter (A) authorizes the project but does not manage compliance. Risk Register (B) tracks risks but does not specifically address compliance. Procurement Plan (C) focuses on vendor management.

questions.q: A project manager discovers that the team is not following the approved quality control processes. What is the best course of action? *

o.t: Conduct a root cause analysis and reinforce quality procedures.
Ignore the issue if the deliverables meet customer expectations.
Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.
Replace team members who are not following procedures.

questions.e: Understanding why quality standards are not followed allows for corrective action. Ignoring the issue (B) can lead to future defects. Escalating (C) and replacing team members (D) are extreme actions that should come later if needed.

questions.q: A project is experiencing frequent changes in stakeholder requirements. What is the best approach to manage these changes? *

o.t: Strictly enforce the baseline scope and reject changes.
Implement an iterative approach and prioritize requirements.
Escalate the issue to the steering committee.
Increase contingency reserves to accommodate changes.

questions.e: Iterative approaches (e.g., Agile) help manage evolving requirements. Strictly enforcing scope (A) may lead to stakeholder dissatisfaction. Escalating (C) should be done only if necessary. Increasing reserves (D) does not solve the root problem.

questions.q: A project team is using Agile, and the product owner is frequently reprioritizing backlog items, causing confusion. What should the Scrum Master do? *

o.t: Lock the backlog to prevent further changes.
Educate the product owner on proper backlog refinement practices.
Allow the development team to decide priorities.
Extend sprint durations to accommodate changing priorities.

questions.e: The backlog should be refined collaboratively to avoid disruption. Locking the backlog (A) goes against Agile flexibility. Letting the team decide priorities (C) is not their role. Extending sprints (D) contradicts Agile principles.
